# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# masl_bytecode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/masl_bytecode/1.0.0/masl_bytecode/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#masl_bytecode)masl_bytecode

Bytecode serializer for the MASL compiler.

Serializes an IR Document into the `.mdkc` binary format.

Binary layout:

- Magic header: “MDKC” (4 bytes)
- Format version: u32 little-endian
- Schema version: u32 little-endian
- Namespace string index: u32 little-endian
- xxHash64 checksum: u64 little-endian
- String table
- Subject table
- Resource table
- Expression pool

See RFC-0014 — Binary Format (.mdkc).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [FORMAT_](https://docs.rs/constant.FORMAT_VERSION.html)- VERSION
- The current binary format version.
- [MAGIC](https://docs.rs/constant.MAGIC.html)
- The MASL binary magic bytes: ASCII “MDKC”

# car_policy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/car-policy/0.32.0/car_policy/

## Expand description

Policy engine — rules that govern what actions the runtime will allow.

Two complementary mechanisms live here:

- `PolicyEngine`- `(Action, StateStore)`and collects every violation. Designed for pre-execution batch validation.
- `inspectors::InspectorChain`- `(tool_name, params)`at dispatch time. Stops on the first Deny. Designed for hot-path guardrails (egress, repetition, adversary review).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use flow_gate::`- [enforce_flow](https://docs.rs/flow_gate/fn.enforce_flow.html);
- `pub use flow_gate::`- [flow_fingerprint](https://docs.rs/flow_gate/fn.flow_fingerprint.html);
- `pub use flow_gate::`- [FlowEnforcement](https://docs.rs/flow_gate/struct.FlowEnforcement.html);
- `pub use flow_gate::`- [PendingFlowApproval](https://docs.rs/flow_gate/struct.PendingFlowApproval.html);
- `pub use intent_gate::`- [enforce_intent](https://docs.rs/intent_gate/fn.enforce_intent.html);
- `pub use intent_gate::`- [intent_fingerprint](https://docs.rs/intent_gate/fn.intent_fingerprint.html);
- `pub use intent_gate::`- [IntentEnforcement](https://docs.rs/intent_gate/struct.IntentEnforcement.html);
- `pub use intent_gate::`- [PendingIntentApproval](https://docs.rs/intent_gate/struct.PendingIntentApproval.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [flow_](https://docs.rs/flow_gate/index.html)- gate
- HITL bridge for information-flow enforcement (verifiable tool safety, Slice 3).
- [inspectors](https://docs.rs/inspectors/index.html)
- Tool-call inspection pipeline.
- [intent_](https://docs.rs/intent_gate/index.html)- gate
- HITL bridge for intent-grounded verification (VIGIL, arXiv 2601.05755 — Slice 3).
- [permission](https://docs.rs/permission/index.html)
- Permission tiers, risk classification, and human-in-the-loop approval
as **durable harness state**.
- [rules](https://docs.rs/rules/index.html)
- Declarative, project-authored deny rules for the `PolicyEngine`
- [skill_](https://docs.rs/skill_trust/index.html)- trust
- Skill trust & lifecycle governance (arXiv 2602.12430, *Agent Skills for Large Language Models: Architecture, Acquisition, Security, and the Path Forward*).

- Evaluates actions against registered policies.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [backfill_](https://docs.rs/fn.backfill_junction_tables.html)- junction_ - tables
- Backfill one or more junction tables (`works_orcid`,`works_ror`,`works_references`) for every row in`works`.`providers`restricts to specific provider values (e.g.`["Crossref"]`); empty = all providers. Reads blobs in 50 k-row streaming batches; uses`INSERT OR IGNORE`so it is safe to re-run or interrupt and resume. Returns`(works_scanned, rows_inserted)`.
- [backfill_](https://docs.rs/fn.backfill_works_references.html)- works_ - references

- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_pidbox_to_sqlite.html)- pidbox_ - to_ - sqlite
- Stream the pidbox dump (a mixed-source VRAIX SQLite file containing crossref,
datacite, and ROR rows) directly to a commonmeta SQLite database. Each row
is routed to the appropriate parser by its `source_id`; ROR rows are skipped. When`update`is false the output file is recreated; when true rows are upserted by`id`. Returns the number of records written.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_pmc_ids_to_sqlite.html)- pmc_ - ids_ - to_ - sqlite
- Stream a gzip-compressed PMC-ids CSV file into the commonmeta SQLite
database at `output_path`, upserting rows that have a DOI. Pass`limit = 0`to process all rows. Returns the number of records written.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_vraix_to_sqlite.html)- vraix_ - to_ - sqlite
- Stream a VRAIX daily dump at `input_path`directly to a commonmeta SQLite database at`output_path`in batches of 10 000 rows, converting with`from`-specific parser and writing each batch in a single transaction.`limit`caps total records written; pass`0`for all rows. When`update`is false the output file is deleted and recreated (default). When`update`is true the existing file is kept and rows are upserted by their`id`primary key — new rows are inserted, existing rows are replaced. Returns the number of records written. No`Vec<Data>`is held for the whole file — peak memory is proportional to one batch, not the whole dump.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_zst_pidbox_to_sqlite.html)- zst_ - pidbox_ - to_ - sqlite
- Like `stream_pidbox_to_sqlite`
- [upsert_](https://docs.rs/fn.upsert_sqlite.html)- sqlite
- Like `write_sqlite``id`already exists are replaced; new rows are inserted.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_sqlite.html)- sqlite
- Validate records in a commonmeta SQLite database against the v1.0 JSON schema.
- [write](https://docs.rs/fn.write.html)
- Write an already-loaded record to `to`format.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_archive.html)- archive
- Render `list`to`to`format, split into entries of at most`batch_size`records each — suitable for packing into an archive via`io_utils::write_zip_archive``io_utils::write_tar_gz_archive``base_name`(e.g.`"out.json"`) names the single entry directly when there’s only one batch, or gets a numbered suffix (`"out-00000.json"`,`"out-00001.json"`, …) when there are several.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_archive_citation.html)- archive_ - citation
- Like `write_archive`, but passes CSL`style`/`locale`through to the citation writer when`to == "citation"`.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_list.html)- list
- Render a list of records to `to`format as a single buffer: a JSON array for object-shaped formats (`commonmeta`,`csl`,`datacite`,`inveniordm`,`schemaorg`,`ror`), or newline-joined output for line/document-shaped formats (e.g.`bibtex`,`ris`,`crossref_xml`).
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_list_citation.html)- list_ - citation
- Like `write_list`, but passes CSL`style`/`locale`through to the citation writer when`to == "citation"`(ignored for every other format, same as`convert_citation`/`write_citation`).
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_orcid_commonmeta.html)- orcid_ - commonmeta
- Convert ORCID 3.0 person JSON + resolved affiliations + works to a commonmeta
array validated against the commonmeta v1.0 schema. `works`may be empty.

- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_orcid_json.html)- orcid_ - json
- Serialize an ORCID 3.0 person JSON value (from `fetch_orcid_person_json``fetch_orcid_person_json_sqlite`
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_parquet.html)- parquet
- Write a list of commonmeta records as a single Parquet file. Alongside a
flattened tabular projection of each record’s fields (for filtering in
tools like DuckDB without parsing JSON), every row also carries a `json`column with the record’s complete serialization, so`read_parquet`
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_ror_commonmeta.html)- ror_ - commonmeta
- Serialize a ROR organization `Data`as a v1.0-compliant commonmeta JSON array.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_ror_json.html)- ror_ - json
- Write a ROR-derived record as raw ROR-shaped JSON (as opposed to
`write("ror", data)`, which produces InvenioRDM vocabulary YAML).
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_ror_sqlite.html)- ror_ - sqlite
- Write a list of ROR records to a SQLite3 database at `path`with an`organizations`table. Existing file is deleted first. JSON array columns (`types`,`locations`,`names`,`external_ids`) are queryable via SQLite’s`json_each()`. The`metadata`column stores the full ROR JSON as a zstd-compressed BLOB for lossless round-trips.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_ror_v2_json.html)- ror_ - v2_ - json
- Serialize a `Ror`record as ROR v2-compatible JSON, converting empty-string`lang`and`preferred`fields to JSON`null`to match the canonical API output.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_sqlite.html)- sqlite
- Write `list`as a SQLite3 database with a`works`table whose columns mirror the commonmeta v1.0 schema. Simple string fields are stored as TEXT; complex fields are stored as compact JSON TEXT. Any existing file at`path`is deleted first.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_vraix_table_parquet.html)- vraix_ - table_ - parquet
- Write a VRAIX dump’s transport table (e.g. `pid_records`) to a single Parquet file’s bytes, using its raw columns (`pid`,`source_id`,`raw_metadata`, …) as-is —*not*converted to commonmeta`Data`the way`read_vraix_sqlite``batch_size`controls how many rows land in each internal Parquet row group (see [`formats::commonmeta::write_parquet_all`]’s analogous`ROW_GROUP_SIZE`for why this matters for large dumps).
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_with_style.html)- with_ - style
- Like [`write`], but forwards`style`and`locale`to the citation writer. For non-`"citation"`formats both parameters are ignored.

# car-inference

Local and remote model inference for the [Common Agent Runtime](https://github.com/Parslee-ai/car).

## What it does

Provides on-device inference using Candle (Metal on macOS, CUDA on Linux) with Qwen3 models
downloaded from HuggingFace on first use. Also supports remote APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google)
via the same typed `ModelSchema` interface. The `AdaptiveRouter` selects the best model using
a filter-score-explore strategy, learning from outcomes over time via `OutcomeTracker`.

## Usage

```
use ;
let engine = new;
let result = engine.generate.await?;
```
## Apple FoundationModels backend (macOS 26+)

On Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 26 or later with Apple Intelligence
provisioned, CAR can route inference to the **system LLM** through
Apple's FoundationModels framework — no model file to download, no API
key, no model weights. The OS owns everything.

The integration is a small Swift shim
(`car-inference/swift/CarFoundationModels.swift`) compiled by
`build.rs` and linked into the crate. The framework is **weak-linked**
so the produced binary still loads on pre-26 macOS; a runtime
availability check (`is_available()`, cached for 5 seconds) gates
calls.

```
// Routing happens automatically — request the apple/foundation:default
// model id, or let the AdaptiveRouter pick it for you.
let result = engine.generate.await?;
```
The catalog entry is tagged `["builtin", "local", "low_latency", "private"]`.
The adaptive router scores `low_latency` AND `private` together via
`SYSTEM_LLM_BONUS` (0.12) so system-owned models compete fairly with
MLX 4B for short fast-turn tasks (autocomplete, summarize, classify)
without claiming heavy reasoning workloads they can't serve.

**What's wired:**

- Single-shot text generation via `generate()`
- Token-by-token streaming via `stream()`with prefix-diffing on Apple's cumulative snapshots —`StreamEvent::Done.text`carries the full assembled output, matching Candle/MLX shape.
- Tool calling via `generate_with_tools()`— JSON-Schema tool definitions are converted to per-tool`DynamicGenerationSchema`s so the model sees real schemas. A capture-only Swift`Tool`records the first invocation and ends the turn; the call comes back as the standard`ToolCall`shape the remote backends emit and the runtime executes it (CAR's propose/validate/execute contract). At most one tool call per turn — sequential tool use, no parallel calls; the catalog entry claims`tool_use`but deliberately NOT`multi_tool_call`, the router-readable "no parallel calls" signal. When a call is captured,`text`is empty — pre-call assistant prose is discarded.
- Structured output via `generate_structured()`—`ResponseFormat::JsonSchema`maps onto FM's native constrained decoding (`respond(to:schema:)`).`JsonObject`has no native FM mode and falls back to instruction injection with a warning.
- Graceful fallthrough on vision / audio / video — returns
`InferenceError::UnsupportedMode`(streaming included) so the router picks the next candidate instead of silently dropping capabilities.

**What isn't:**

- Multimodal input — the public FoundationModels API is text-only.
- Full JSON-Schema fidelity: the `DynamicGenerationSchema`conversion covers object/string/number/integer/boolean/array and string enums; typeless nodes (oneOf/anyOf/$ref), union types (`["number","null"]`), unrecognized types, and non-string enums degrade to permissive string fields (never to an empty object), and numeric enums keep the base type but lose the value constraint. Every degradation is detected on the Rust side and logged via`tracing::warn!`before crossing the FFI.

**Build requirements:**

- Full Xcode (not just Command Line Tools) on the build host —
needed for `xcrun swiftc`and the FoundationModels SDK.
- macOS 15+ deployment floor (overridable via `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`).

Linux and Intel-Mac builds skip the Swift compile entirely; the
`ModelSource::AppleFoundationModels` schema variant still serializes
(so registries can describe the model on any platform), but dispatch
errors out with `UnsupportedMode` before reaching the bridge.

## Crate features

- `metal`-- Apple Silicon GPU acceleration
- `cuda`-- NVIDIA GPU acceleration
- `ast`-- AST-aware code generation via- `car-ast`

Part of [CAR](https://github.com/Parslee-ai/car) -- see the main repo for full documentation.

---

# car_daemon_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/car-daemon-client/0.32.0/car_daemon_client/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#car-daemon-client)car-daemon-client

The WebSocket JSON-RPC client core every CAR FFI binding proxies
through. Extracted verbatim from `car-ffi-common` (which re-exports
these modules, so `car_ffi_common::proxy::…` /
`car_ffi_common::auth_token::…` import paths keep working) so the
UniFFI Swift/Kotlin surface can reach the daemon without absorbing
car-ffi-common’s transitive dependency tree — car-voice
(whisper-rs, coreaudio-sys), car-browser, car-vision, etc. are
wrong for `aarch64-apple-ios` and unnecessary for a pure WS client.

Two modules:

- `proxy`- `proxy::DaemonClient`- `session.auth`+- `server.handshake`connect sequence, server-initiated requests (- `tools.execute`callbacks) via registered handlers, notifications, and per-method read-timeout derivation. Plus the- `proxy_*`per-method wrappers the bindings dispatch to.
- `auth_token`- `0600`, DPAPI-encrypted on Windows;- `$CAR_AUTH_TOKEN`override for cross-host clients).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [auth_](https://docs.rs/auth_token/index.html)- token
- Shared auth-token path resolution and IO for car-server’s per-launch ephemeral handshake (Parslee-ai/car-releases#32).
- [proxy](https://docs.rs/proxy/index.html)
- Thin client to the singleton CAR daemon over WebSocket JSON-RPC.

# car_verify - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/car-verify/0.32.0/car_verify/

## Expand description

Formal verification for Agent IR.

Given a state S and proposal P, you can:

- **verify**: Prove P is satisfiable in S without executing
- **simulate**: Compute expected final state S’ without tools
- **equivalent**: Show two proposals produce identical state
- **optimize**: Reorder actions provably safely

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [concurrency](https://docs.rs/concurrency/index.html)
- Multi-agent concurrency anomalies — detection + consistency level
(arXiv 2606.17182, *Verified Detection and Prevention of Concurrency Anomalies in Multi-Agent Large Language Model Systems*).
- [cwm](https://docs.rs/cwm/index.html)
- Code World Models — trajectory-validated effect models (Slice 1).
- [dag](https://docs.rs/dag/index.html)
- Shared DAG helpers for the verify family.
- [infoflow](https://docs.rs/infoflow/index.html)
- Static information-flow + tool-sequence safety checks over a plan.
- [intent](https://docs.rs/intent/index.html)
- Intent-grounded action verification (arXiv 2601.05755, *VIGIL: Defending LLM Agents Against Tool Stream Injection via Verify-Before-Commit*).
- [plan_](https://docs.rs/plan_check/index.html)- check
- Symbolic plan precondition verification (arXiv 2603.14730, *GNNVerifier: Graph-based Verifier for LLM Task Planning*; pre-execution premise shared with*VerifyLLM*, arXiv 2507.05118).
- [transaction](https://docs.rs/transaction/index.html)
- Transactional conflict detection for shared program state.
- [workflow_](https://docs.rs/workflow_graph/index.html)- graph
- Static workflow-graph verification — structural checks + witnesses
(arXiv 2603.20356, *Agentproof: Static Verification of Agent Workflow Graphs*).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [equivalent](https://docs.rs/fn.equivalent.html)
- Test if two proposals produce identical state transitions.
- [optimize](https://docs.rs/fn.optimize.html)
- Optimize a proposal: remove phantom dependencies to enable more parallelism.
- [simulate](https://docs.rs/fn.simulate.html)
- Simulate a proposal’s state effects without executing tools.
- [verify](https://docs.rs/fn.verify.html)
- Statically verify a proposal against an initial state.
- [verify_](https://docs.rs/fn.verify_with_schemas.html)- with_ - schemas
- Like `verify``tool_call`’s`parameters`against the registered`ToolSchema``parameters`JSON Schema — catching type mismatches (`{"path": 42}`for a`string`param) and missing`required`fields before dispatch. Tool existence is checked against the schema map’s keys. This is the path the runtime (`verify_proposal`) and daemon (`verify`JSON-RPC) use, where the full schemas registered via`register_tool_schema`are available.

# car_ui_agent - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/car-ui-agent/0.32.0/car_ui_agent/

## Expand description

In-process UI-improvement agent for the adaptive A2UI rendering
loop. Consumes `RenderReport` telemetry from the renderer
(Parslee-ai/car#180), runs a library of rendering strategies, and
returns a `Decision` (typically a `PatchComponents` envelope) the
caller routes through `car-a2ui`’s surface store.

The agent is structured as a library, not a service. Pattern
mirrors `car-meeting::MemgineIngestSink`: a struct with a sync
callback that the runtime invokes from its async context. No A2A
observer registration; no outbound emission code — the call site
in `car-server-core` routes the returned envelope through the
existing surface store apply path.

Reference Swift shape:
`a2ui-shader/Sources/A2UIShaderAgent/UIImprovementAgent.swift`.
Loop semantics — `in_response_to` correlation, hard-stop on
`placeholder_count > 0`, stability-window termination, no double-
patch at the same sequence — port across without change.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use agent::`- [UIImprovementAgent](https://docs.rs/agent/struct.UIImprovementAgent.html);
- `pub use errors::`- [UIAgentError](https://docs.rs/errors/enum.UIAgentError.html);
- `pub use strategies::`- [BuiltInStrategies](https://docs.rs/strategies/struct.BuiltInStrategies.html);
- `pub use strategies::`- [CompactDenseColumn](https://docs.rs/strategies/struct.CompactDenseColumn.html);
- `pub use strategies::`- [RenderingStrategy](https://docs.rs/strategies/trait.RenderingStrategy.html);
- `pub use strategies::`- [TagSmallListDomain](https://docs.rs/strategies/struct.TagSmallListDomain.html);
- `pub use types::`- [Decision](https://docs.rs/types/enum.Decision.html);
- `pub use types::`- [IntentSignature](https://docs.rs/types/struct.IntentSignature.html);

# objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/objc-sys/0.3.5/target-redirect/x86_64-apple-darwin/objc_sys/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#raw-bindings-to-objective-c-runtimes)Raw bindings to Objective-C runtimes

These bindings contain almost no documentation, so it is highly
recommended to read Apple’s [documentation about the Objective-C
runtime](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Cocoa/Conceptual/ObjCRuntimeGuide/Introduction/Introduction.html), Apple’s [runtime reference](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/objectivec/objective-c_runtime?language=objc), or to use
`objc2::runtime` which provides a higher-level API.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-support)Runtime Support

Objective-C has a runtime, different implementations of said runtime
exist, and they act in slightly different ways. By default, Apple
platforms link to Apple’s runtime, but if you’re using another runtime you
must tell it to this library using feature flags (you might have to
disable the default `apple` feature first).

One could ask, why even bother supporting other runtimes? For me, the
primary reasoning iss *robustness*. By testing with these alternative
runtimes in CI, we become by extension much more confident that our
implementation doesn’t rely on brittle unspecified behaviour, and works
across different macOS and iOS versions.

- Feature flag: `apple`.

This is used by default, and has the highest support priority (all of
`objc2` will work with this runtime).

The supported runtime version (higher versions lets the compiler enable
newer optimizations, at the cost of not supporting older operating
systems) can be chosen using the standard `X_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`
environment variables:

- macOS: `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`10.12`,`11.0`on Aarch64.
- iOS / iPadOS: `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`10.0`.
- tvOS: `TVOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`10.0`.
- watchOS: `WATCHOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`5.0`.

The default (and minimum) versions are the [same as those Rust itself
has](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.74.0/compiler/rustc_target/src/spec/apple_base.rs).

- Feature flag: `gnustep-1-7`,`gnustep-1-8`,`gnustep-1-9`,`gnustep-2-0`and`gnustep-2-1`depending on the version you’re using.

- Feature flag: `unstable-winobjc`.

**Unstable: Hasn’t been tested on Windows yet!**

[A fork](https://github.com/microsoft/libobjc2) based on GNUStep’s
`libobjc2` version 1.8, with very few user-facing changes.

- Feature flag: `unstable-objfw`.

**Unstable: Doesn’t work yet!**

TODO.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-runtimes)Other runtimes

This library will probably only ever support [“Modern”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objective-C#Modern_Objective-C)
Objective-C runtimes, since support for reference-counting primitives like
`objc_retain` and `objc_autoreleasePoolPop` is a vital requirement for
most applications.

This rules out the GCC [ libobjc](https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/tree/master/libobjc) runtime (see

[this](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Standards.html#Objective-C-and-Objective-C_002b_002b-Languages)), the

[runtime and](https://github.com/mulle-objc/mulle-objc-runtime)

`mulle-objc`[cocotron](https://cocotron.org/). (But support for

[may be added). More information on different runtimes can be found in GNUStep’s](https://github.com/darlinghq/darling-objc4)

`darling`[Objective-C Compiler and Runtime FAQ](http://wiki.gnustep.org/index.php/Objective-C_Compiler_and_Runtime_FAQ).

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-linking-configuration)Advanced linking configuration

This crate defines the `links` key in `Cargo.toml` so it’s possible to
change the linking to `libobjc`, see [the relevant cargo
docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html#overriding-build-scripts).

In the future, this crate may vendor the required source code to automatically build and link to the runtimes. Choosing static vs. dynamic linking here may also become an option.

[§](https://docs.rs#objective-c-compiler-configuration)Objective-C Compiler configuration

Objective-C compilers like `clang` and `gcc` requires configuring the
calling ABI to the runtime you’re using:

- `clang`uses the- `-fobjc-runtime`- [options](https://clang.llvm.org/doxygen/classclang_1_1ObjCRuntime.html#af19fe070a7073df4ecc666b44137c4e5).
- `gcc`uses the- `-fgnu-runtime`or- `-fnext-runtime`

This is relevant if you’re building and linking to custom Objective-C
sources in a build script. To assist in compiling Objective-C sources,
this crate’s  build script expose the `DEP_OBJC_0_3_CC_ARGS` environment
variable to downstream build scripts.

Example usage in your `build.rs` (using the `cc` crate) would be as
follows:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    let mut builder = cc::Build::new();
    builder.compiler("clang");
    builder.file("my_objective_c_script.m");
    for flag in std::env::var("DEP_OBJC_0_3_CC_ARGS").unwrap().split(' ') {
        builder.flag(flag);
    }
    builder.compile("libmy_objective_c_script.a");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#design-choices)Design choices

It is recognized that the most primary consumer of this library will be
macOS and secondly iOS applications. Therefore it was chosen not to use
`bindgen` 1 in our build script to not add compilation cost to those
targets.

Deprecated functions are also not included for future compability, since they could be removed in any macOS release, and then our code would break. If you have a need for these, please open an issue and we can discuss it!

Some items (in particular the `objc_msgSend_X` family) have `cfg`s that
prevent their usage on different platforms; these are **semver-stable** in
the sense that they will only get less restrictive, never more.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/objc-sys/0.3.5/target-redirect/x86_64-apple-ios/objc_sys/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#raw-bindings-to-objective-c-runtimes)Raw bindings to Objective-C runtimes

These bindings contain almost no documentation, so it is highly
recommended to read Apple’s [documentation about the Objective-C
runtime](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Cocoa/Conceptual/ObjCRuntimeGuide/Introduction/Introduction.html), Apple’s [runtime reference](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/objectivec/objective-c_runtime?language=objc), or to use
`objc2::runtime` which provides a higher-level API.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-support)Runtime Support

Objective-C has a runtime, different implementations of said runtime
exist, and they act in slightly different ways. By default, Apple
platforms link to Apple’s runtime, but if you’re using another runtime you
must tell it to this library using feature flags (you might have to
disable the default `apple` feature first).

One could ask, why even bother supporting other runtimes? For me, the
primary reasoning iss *robustness*. By testing with these alternative
runtimes in CI, we become by extension much more confident that our
implementation doesn’t rely on brittle unspecified behaviour, and works
across different macOS and iOS versions.

- Feature flag: `apple`.

This is used by default, and has the highest support priority (all of
`objc2` will work with this runtime).

The supported runtime version (higher versions lets the compiler enable
newer optimizations, at the cost of not supporting older operating
systems) can be chosen using the standard `X_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`
environment variables:

- macOS: `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`10.12`,`11.0`on Aarch64.
- iOS / iPadOS: `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`10.0`.
- tvOS: `TVOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`10.0`.
- watchOS: `WATCHOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`5.0`.

The default (and minimum) versions are the [same as those Rust itself
has](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.74.0/compiler/rustc_target/src/spec/apple_base.rs).

- Feature flag: `gnustep-1-7`,`gnustep-1-8`,`gnustep-1-9`,`gnustep-2-0`and`gnustep-2-1`depending on the version you’re using.

- Feature flag: `unstable-winobjc`.

**Unstable: Hasn’t been tested on Windows yet!**

[A fork](https://github.com/microsoft/libobjc2) based on GNUStep’s
`libobjc2` version 1.8, with very few user-facing changes.

- Feature flag: `unstable-objfw`.

**Unstable: Doesn’t work yet!**

TODO.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-runtimes)Other runtimes

This library will probably only ever support [“Modern”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objective-C#Modern_Objective-C)
Objective-C runtimes, since support for reference-counting primitives like
`objc_retain` and `objc_autoreleasePoolPop` is a vital requirement for
most applications.

This rules out the GCC [ libobjc](https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/tree/master/libobjc) runtime (see

[this](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Standards.html#Objective-C-and-Objective-C_002b_002b-Languages)), the

[runtime and](https://github.com/mulle-objc/mulle-objc-runtime)

`mulle-objc`[cocotron](https://cocotron.org/). (But support for

[may be added). More information on different runtimes can be found in GNUStep’s](https://github.com/darlinghq/darling-objc4)

`darling`[Objective-C Compiler and Runtime FAQ](http://wiki.gnustep.org/index.php/Objective-C_Compiler_and_Runtime_FAQ).

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-linking-configuration)Advanced linking configuration

This crate defines the `links` key in `Cargo.toml` so it’s possible to
change the linking to `libobjc`, see [the relevant cargo
docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html#overriding-build-scripts).

In the future, this crate may vendor the required source code to automatically build and link to the runtimes. Choosing static vs. dynamic linking here may also become an option.

[§](https://docs.rs#objective-c-compiler-configuration)Objective-C Compiler configuration

Objective-C compilers like `clang` and `gcc` requires configuring the
calling ABI to the runtime you’re using:

- `clang`uses the- `-fobjc-runtime`- [options](https://clang.llvm.org/doxygen/classclang_1_1ObjCRuntime.html#af19fe070a7073df4ecc666b44137c4e5).
- `gcc`uses the- `-fgnu-runtime`or- `-fnext-runtime`

This is relevant if you’re building and linking to custom Objective-C
sources in a build script. To assist in compiling Objective-C sources,
this crate’s  build script expose the `DEP_OBJC_0_3_CC_ARGS` environment
variable to downstream build scripts.

Example usage in your `build.rs` (using the `cc` crate) would be as
follows:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    let mut builder = cc::Build::new();
    builder.compiler("clang");
    builder.file("my_objective_c_script.m");
    for flag in std::env::var("DEP_OBJC_0_3_CC_ARGS").unwrap().split(' ') {
        builder.flag(flag);
    }
    builder.compile("libmy_objective_c_script.a");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#design-choices)Design choices

It is recognized that the most primary consumer of this library will be
macOS and secondly iOS applications. Therefore it was chosen not to use
`bindgen` 1 in our build script to not add compilation cost to those
targets.

Deprecated functions are also not included for future compability, since they could be removed in any macOS release, and then our code would break. If you have a need for these, please open an issue and we can discuss it!

Some items (in particular the `objc_msgSend_X` family) have `cfg`s that
prevent their usage on different platforms; these are **semver-stable** in
the sense that they will only get less restrictive, never more.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_class.html)- class
- An opaque type that represents an Objective-C class.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_ivar.html)- ivar
- An opaque type that represents an instance variable.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_method.html)- method
- A type that represents a method in a class definition.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_method_description.html)- method_ - description
- Describes an Objective-C method.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_object.html)- object
- An opaque type that represents an object / an instance of a class.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_property.html)- property
- An opaque type that describes a property in a class.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_property_attribute_t.html)- property_ - attribute_ - t
- Describes an Objective-C property attribute.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_protocol.html)- protocol
- Opaque type for Objective-C protocols.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_selector.html)- selector
- An opaque type that represents a method selector.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_super.html)- super
- Specifies data used when sending messages to superclasses.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

# objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/objc-sys/0.3.5/target-redirect/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/objc_sys/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#raw-bindings-to-objective-c-runtimes)Raw bindings to Objective-C runtimes

These bindings contain almost no documentation, so it is highly
recommended to read Apple’s [documentation about the Objective-C
runtime](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Cocoa/Conceptual/ObjCRuntimeGuide/Introduction/Introduction.html), Apple’s [runtime reference](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/objectivec/objective-c_runtime?language=objc), or to use
`objc2::runtime` which provides a higher-level API.

[§](https://docs.rs#runtime-support)Runtime Support

Objective-C has a runtime, different implementations of said runtime
exist, and they act in slightly different ways. By default, Apple
platforms link to Apple’s runtime, but if you’re using another runtime you
must tell it to this library using feature flags (you might have to
disable the default `apple` feature first).

One could ask, why even bother supporting other runtimes? For me, the
primary reasoning iss *robustness*. By testing with these alternative
runtimes in CI, we become by extension much more confident that our
implementation doesn’t rely on brittle unspecified behaviour, and works
across different macOS and iOS versions.

- Feature flag: `apple`.

This is used by default, and has the highest support priority (all of
`objc2` will work with this runtime).

The supported runtime version (higher versions lets the compiler enable
newer optimizations, at the cost of not supporting older operating
systems) can be chosen using the standard `X_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`
environment variables:

- macOS: `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`10.12`,`11.0`on Aarch64.
- iOS / iPadOS: `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`10.0`.
- tvOS: `TVOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`10.0`.
- watchOS: `WATCHOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default`5.0`.

The default (and minimum) versions are the [same as those Rust itself
has](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.74.0/compiler/rustc_target/src/spec/apple_base.rs).

- Feature flag: `gnustep-1-7`,`gnustep-1-8`,`gnustep-1-9`,`gnustep-2-0`and`gnustep-2-1`depending on the version you’re using.

- Feature flag: `unstable-winobjc`.

**Unstable: Hasn’t been tested on Windows yet!**

[A fork](https://github.com/microsoft/libobjc2) based on GNUStep’s
`libobjc2` version 1.8, with very few user-facing changes.

- Feature flag: `unstable-objfw`.

**Unstable: Doesn’t work yet!**

TODO.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-runtimes)Other runtimes

This library will probably only ever support [“Modern”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objective-C#Modern_Objective-C)
Objective-C runtimes, since support for reference-counting primitives like
`objc_retain` and `objc_autoreleasePoolPop` is a vital requirement for
most applications.

This rules out the GCC [ libobjc](https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/tree/master/libobjc) runtime (see

[this](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Standards.html#Objective-C-and-Objective-C_002b_002b-Languages)), the

[runtime and](https://github.com/mulle-objc/mulle-objc-runtime)

`mulle-objc`[cocotron](https://cocotron.org/). (But support for

[may be added). More information on different runtimes can be found in GNUStep’s](https://github.com/darlinghq/darling-objc4)

`darling`[Objective-C Compiler and Runtime FAQ](http://wiki.gnustep.org/index.php/Objective-C_Compiler_and_Runtime_FAQ).

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-linking-configuration)Advanced linking configuration

This crate defines the `links` key in `Cargo.toml` so it’s possible to
change the linking to `libobjc`, see [the relevant cargo
docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html#overriding-build-scripts).

In the future, this crate may vendor the required source code to automatically build and link to the runtimes. Choosing static vs. dynamic linking here may also become an option.

[§](https://docs.rs#objective-c-compiler-configuration)Objective-C Compiler configuration

Objective-C compilers like `clang` and `gcc` requires configuring the
calling ABI to the runtime you’re using:

- `clang`uses the- `-fobjc-runtime`- [options](https://clang.llvm.org/doxygen/classclang_1_1ObjCRuntime.html#af19fe070a7073df4ecc666b44137c4e5).
- `gcc`uses the- `-fgnu-runtime`or- `-fnext-runtime`

This is relevant if you’re building and linking to custom Objective-C
sources in a build script. To assist in compiling Objective-C sources,
this crate’s  build script expose the `DEP_OBJC_0_3_CC_ARGS` environment
variable to downstream build scripts.

Example usage in your `build.rs` (using the `cc` crate) would be as
follows:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    let mut builder = cc::Build::new();
    builder.compiler("clang");
    builder.file("my_objective_c_script.m");
    for flag in std::env::var("DEP_OBJC_0_3_CC_ARGS").unwrap().split(' ') {
        builder.flag(flag);
    }
    builder.compile("libmy_objective_c_script.a");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#design-choices)Design choices

It is recognized that the most primary consumer of this library will be
macOS and secondly iOS applications. Therefore it was chosen not to use
`bindgen` 1 in our build script to not add compilation cost to those
targets.

Deprecated functions are also not included for future compability, since they could be removed in any macOS release, and then our code would break. If you have a need for these, please open an issue and we can discuss it!

Some items (in particular the `objc_msgSend_X` family) have `cfg`s that
prevent their usage on different platforms; these are **semver-stable** in
the sense that they will only get less restrictive, never more.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_class.html)- class
- An opaque type that represents an Objective-C class.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_ivar.html)- ivar
- An opaque type that represents an instance variable.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_method.html)- method
- A type that represents a method in a class definition.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_method_description.html)- method_ - description
- Describes an Objective-C method.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_object.html)- object
- An opaque type that represents an object / an instance of a class.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_property.html)- property
- An opaque type that describes a property in a class.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_property_attribute_t.html)- property_ - attribute_ - t
- Describes an Objective-C property attribute.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_protocol.html)- protocol
- Opaque type for Objective-C protocols.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_selector.html)- selector
- An opaque type that represents a method selector.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_super.html)- super
- Specifies data used when sending messages to superclasses.

- Specifies that the associated object is copied.
- [OBJC_](https://docs.rs/constant.OBJC_ASSOCIATION_COPY_NONATOMIC.html)- ASSOCIATION_ - COPY_ - NONATOMIC
- Specifies that the associated object is copied.

- Specifies a strong reference to the associated object.
- [OBJC_](https://docs.rs/constant.OBJC_ASSOCIATION_RETAIN_NONATOMIC.html)- ASSOCIATION_ - RETAIN_ - NONATOMIC
- Specifies a strong reference to the associated object.

- Only relevant before macOS 10.13

- A quick alias for a `null_mut`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [BOOL](https://docs.rs/type.BOOL.html)
- The Objective-C `BOOL`type.
- [IMP](https://docs.rs/type.IMP.html)
- A nullable pointer to the start of a method implementation.
- [NSInteger](https://docs.rs/type.NSInteger.html)
- A signed integer value type.
- [NSUInteger](https://docs.rs/type.NSUInteger.html)
- Describes an unsigned integer.
- [SEL](https://docs.rs/type.SEL.html)
- An immutable pointer to a selector.
- [id](https://docs.rs/type.id.html)
- A mutable pointer to an object / instance.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/type.objc_AssociationPolicy.html)- Association - Policy
- Policies related to associative references.
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/type.objc_exception_handler.html)- exception_ - handler - Apple and macOS and non-x86
- Remember that this is non-null!
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/type.objc_exception_matcher.html)- exception_ - matcher - Apple and not (macOS and x86)
- Remember that this is non-null!
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/type.objc_exception_preprocessor.html)- exception_ - preprocessor - Apple and not (macOS and x86)
- Remember that this is non-null!
- [objc_](https://docs.rs/type.objc_uncaught_exception_handler.html)- uncaught_ - exception_ - handler - Apple and not (macOS and x86)
- Remember that this is non-null!

# objc-sys

[main library docs](https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/objc_sys/),

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/src/objc_sys/lib.rs.html

# objc_sys/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # Raw bindings to Objective-C runtimes
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! These bindings contain almost no documentation, so it is highly
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! recommended to read Apple's [documentation about the Objective-C
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! runtime][runtime-guide], Apple's [runtime reference][apple], or to use
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! `objc2::runtime` which provides a higher-level API.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! [runtime-guide]: https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Cocoa/Conceptual/ObjCRuntimeGuide/Introduction/Introduction.html
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! [apple]: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/objectivec/objective-c_runtime?language=objc
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! ## Runtime Support
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! Objective-C has a runtime, different implementations of said runtime
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! exist, and they act in slightly different ways. By default, Apple
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! platforms link to Apple's runtime, but if you're using another runtime you
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! must tell it to this library using feature flags (you might have to
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! disable the default `apple` feature first).
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! One could ask, why even bother supporting other runtimes? For me, the
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! primary reasoning iss _robustness_. By testing with these alternative
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! runtimes in CI, we become by extension much more confident that our
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! implementation doesn't rely on brittle unspecified behaviour, and works
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! across different macOS and iOS versions.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! ### Apple's [`objc4`](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/objc4)
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! - Feature flag: `apple`.
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! This is used by default, and has the highest support priority (all of
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! `objc2` will work with this runtime).
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! The supported runtime version (higher versions lets the compiler enable
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! newer optimizations, at the cost of not supporting older operating
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! systems) can be chosen using the standard `X_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! environment variables:
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! - macOS: `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default `10.12`, `11.0` on Aarch64.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! - iOS / iPadOS: `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default `10.0`.
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! - tvOS: `TVOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default `10.0`.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! - watchOS: `WATCHOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, default `5.0`.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! The default (and minimum) versions are the [same as those Rust itself
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! has][rust-apple-spec].
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! [rust-apple-spec]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.74.0/compiler/rustc_target/src/spec/apple_base.rs
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! ### GNUStep's [`libobjc2`](https://github.com/gnustep/libobjc2)
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! - Feature flag: `gnustep-1-7`, `gnustep-1-8`, `gnustep-1-9`, `gnustep-2-0`
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!   and `gnustep-2-1` depending on the version you're using.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! ### Microsoft's [`WinObjC`](https://github.com/microsoft/WinObjC)
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! - Feature flag: `unstable-winobjc`.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! **Unstable: Hasn't been tested on Windows yet!**
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! [A fork](https://github.com/microsoft/libobjc2) based on GNUStep's
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! `libobjc2` version 1.8, with very few user-facing changes.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! ### [`ObjFW`](https://github.com/ObjFW/ObjFW)
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! - Feature flag: `unstable-objfw`.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! **Unstable: Doesn't work yet!**
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! TODO.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! ### Other runtimes
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! This library will probably only ever support ["Modern"][modern]
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! Objective-C runtimes, since support for reference-counting primitives like
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! `objc_retain` and `objc_autoreleasePoolPop` is a vital requirement for
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! most applications.
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! This rules out the GCC [`libobjc`][gcc-libobjc] runtime (see
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! [this][gcc-objc-support]), the [`mulle-objc`] runtime and [cocotron]. (But
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! support for [`darling`] may be added). More information on different
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! runtimes can be found in GNUStep's [Objective-C Compiler and Runtime
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! FAQ][gnustep-faq].
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! [modern]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objective-C#Modern_Objective-C
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! [gcc-libobjc]: https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/tree/master/libobjc
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! [gcc-objc-support]: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Standards.html#Objective-C-and-Objective-C_002b_002b-Languages
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! [`mulle-objc`]: https://github.com/mulle-objc/mulle-objc-runtime
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! [cocotron]: https://cocotron.org/
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! [`darling`]: https://github.com/darlinghq/darling-objc4
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! [gnustep-faq]: http://wiki.gnustep.org/index.php/Objective-C_Compiler_and_Runtime_FAQ
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! ## Advanced linking configuration
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! This crate defines the `links` key in `Cargo.toml` so it's possible to
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! change the linking to `libobjc`, see [the relevant cargo
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! docs][overriding].
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! In the future, this crate may vendor the required source code to
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! automatically build and link to the runtimes. Choosing static vs. dynamic
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! linking here may also become an option.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! [overriding]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html#overriding-build-scripts
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! ## Objective-C Compiler configuration
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! Objective-C compilers like `clang` and `gcc` requires configuring the
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! calling ABI to the runtime you're using:
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! - `clang` uses the [`-fobjc-runtime`] flag, of which there are a few
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!   different [options][clang-objc-kinds].
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! - `gcc` uses the [`-fgnu-runtime` or `-fnext-runtime`][gcc-flags] options.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!   Note that Modern Objective-C features are ill supported.
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! This is relevant if you're building and linking to custom Objective-C
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! sources in a build script. To assist in compiling Objective-C sources,
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! this crate's  build script expose the `DEP_OBJC_0_3_CC_ARGS` environment
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! variable to downstream build scripts.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! Example usage in your `build.rs` (using the `cc` crate) would be as
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! follows:
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! ```ignore
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! fn main() {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!     let mut builder = cc::Build::new();
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!     builder.compiler("clang");
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!     builder.file("my_objective_c_script.m");
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!     for flag in std::env::var("DEP_OBJC_0_3_CC_ARGS").unwrap().split(' ') {
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!         builder.flag(flag);
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!     }
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!     builder.compile("libmy_objective_c_script.a");
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! }
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! ```
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! [`-fobjc-runtime`]: https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangCommandLineReference.html#cmdoption-clang-fobjc-runtime
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! [clang-objc-kinds]: https://clang.llvm.org/doxygen/classclang_1_1ObjCRuntime.html#af19fe070a7073df4ecc666b44137c4e5
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! [gcc-flags]: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Objective-C-and-Objective-C_002b_002b-Dialect-Options.html
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! ## Design choices
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! It is recognized that the most primary consumer of this library will be
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! macOS and secondly iOS applications. Therefore it was chosen not to use
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! `bindgen`[^1] in our build script to not add compilation cost to those
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! targets.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! Deprecated functions are also not included for future compability, since
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! they could be removed in any macOS release, and then our code would break.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! If you have a need for these, please open an issue and we can discuss it!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! Some items (in particular the `objc_msgSend_X` family) have `cfg`s that
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! prevent their usage on different platforms; these are **semver-stable** in
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! the sense that they will only get less restrictive, never more.
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! [^1]: That said, most of this is created with the help of `bindgen`'s
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! commandline interface, so huge thanks to them!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)
[164](https://docs.rs#164)#![no_std]
[165](https://docs.rs#165)#![warn(clippy::missing_errors_doc)]
[166](https://docs.rs#166)#![warn(clippy::missing_panics_doc)]
[167](https://docs.rs#167)#![allow(clippy::upper_case_acronyms)]
[168](https://docs.rs#168)#![allow(non_camel_case_types)]
[169](https://docs.rs#169)#![allow(non_upper_case_globals)]
[170](https://docs.rs#170)#![allow(non_snake_case)]
[171](https://docs.rs#171)#![allow(missing_debug_implementations)]
[172](https://docs.rs#172)#![doc(html_root_url = "https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5")]
[173](https://docs.rs#173)#![cfg_attr(feature = "unstable-c-unwind", feature(c_unwind))]
[174](https://docs.rs#174)#![cfg_attr(docsrs, feature(doc_auto_cfg, doc_cfg_hide))]
[175](https://docs.rs#175)#![cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg_hide(doc)))]
[176](https://docs.rs#176)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)// TODO: Remove this and add "no-std" category to Cargo.toml
[178](https://docs.rs#178)// Requires a better solution for C-types in `no_std` crates.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)// See https://github.com/japaric/cty/issues/14.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)extern crate std;
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)#[cfg(not(feature = "std"))]
[183](https://docs.rs#183)compile_error!("The `std` feature currently must be enabled.");

[187](https://docs.rs#187)
[188](https://docs.rs#188)macro_rules! generate_linking_tests {
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    {
[190](https://docs.rs#190)        extern $abi:literal {$(
[191](https://docs.rs#191)            $(#[$m:meta])*
[192](https://docs.rs#192)            $v:vis fn $name:ident(
[193](https://docs.rs#193)                $($(#[$a_m:meta])* $a:ident: $t:ty),* $(,)?
[194](https://docs.rs#194)            ) $(-> $r:ty)?;
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        )+}
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        mod $test_name:ident;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    } => {
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        extern $abi {$(
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            $(#[$m])*
[200](https://docs.rs#200)            $v fn $name($($(#[$a_m])* $a: $t),*) $(-> $r)?;
[201](https://docs.rs#201)        )+}
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)        #[allow(deprecated)]
[204](https://docs.rs#204)        #[cfg(test)]
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        mod $test_name {
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            #[allow(unused)]
[207](https://docs.rs#207)            use super::*;
[208](https://docs.rs#208)
[209](https://docs.rs#209)            $(
[210](https://docs.rs#210)                $(#[$m])*
[211](https://docs.rs#211)                #[test]
[212](https://docs.rs#212)                fn $name() {
[213](https://docs.rs#213)                    // Get function pointer to make the linker require the
[214](https://docs.rs#214)                    // symbol to be available.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)                    let f: unsafe extern $abi fn($($(#[$a_m])* $t),*) $(-> $r)? = crate::$name;
[216](https://docs.rs#216)                    // Workaround for https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/92964
[217](https://docs.rs#217)                    #[cfg(feature = "unstable-c-unwind")]
[218](https://docs.rs#218)                    #[allow(clippy::useless_transmute)]
[219](https://docs.rs#219)                    let f: unsafe extern "C" fn() = unsafe { core::mem::transmute(f) };
[220](https://docs.rs#220)                    // Execute side-effect to ensure it is not optimized away.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)                    std::println!("{:p}", f);
[222](https://docs.rs#222)                }
[223](https://docs.rs#223)            )+
[224](https://docs.rs#224)        }
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    };
[226](https://docs.rs#226)}
[227](https://docs.rs#227)
[228](https://docs.rs#228)macro_rules! extern_c {
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    {
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        $(
[231](https://docs.rs#231)            $(#[$m:meta])*
[232](https://docs.rs#232)            $v:vis fn $name:ident(
[233](https://docs.rs#233)                $($(#[$a_m:meta])* $a:ident: $t:ty),* $(,)?
[234](https://docs.rs#234)            ) $(-> $r:ty)?;
[235](https://docs.rs#235)        )+
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    } => {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        generate_linking_tests! {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)            extern "C" {$(
[239](https://docs.rs#239)                $(#[$m])*
[240](https://docs.rs#240)                $v fn $name($($(#[$a_m])* $a: $t),*) $(-> $r)?;
[241](https://docs.rs#241)            )+}
[242](https://docs.rs#242)            mod test_linkable;
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    };
[245](https://docs.rs#245)}
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)// A lot of places may call `+initialize`, but the runtime guards those calls
[248](https://docs.rs#248)// with `@try/@catch` blocks already, so we don't need to mark every function
[249](https://docs.rs#249)// "C-unwind", only certain ones!
[250](https://docs.rs#250)macro_rules! extern_c_unwind {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        $(
[253](https://docs.rs#253)            $(#[$m:meta])*
[254](https://docs.rs#254)            $v:vis fn $name:ident(
[255](https://docs.rs#255)                $($(#[$a_m:meta])* $a:ident: $t:ty),* $(,)?
[256](https://docs.rs#256)            ) $(-> $r:ty)?;
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        )+
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    } => {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        #[cfg(not(feature = "unstable-c-unwind"))]
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        generate_linking_tests! {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)            extern "C" {$(
[262](https://docs.rs#262)                $(#[$m])*
[263](https://docs.rs#263)                $v fn $name($($(#[$a_m])* $a: $t),*) $(-> $r)?;
[264](https://docs.rs#264)            )+}
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            mod test_linkable_unwind;
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        }
[267](https://docs.rs#267)
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        #[cfg(feature = "unstable-c-unwind")]
[269](https://docs.rs#269)        generate_linking_tests! {
[270](https://docs.rs#270)            extern "C-unwind" {$(
[271](https://docs.rs#271)                $(#[$m])*
[272](https://docs.rs#272)                $v fn $name($($(#[$a_m])* $a: $t),*) $(-> $r)?;
[273](https://docs.rs#273)            )+}
[274](https://docs.rs#274)            mod test_linkable_unwind;
[275](https://docs.rs#275)        }
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    };
[277](https://docs.rs#277)}

[309](https://docs.rs#309)/// We don't know much about the actual structs, so better mark them `!Send`,
[310](https://docs.rs#310)/// `!Sync`, `!UnwindSafe`, `!RefUnwindSafe`, `!Unpin` and as mutable behind
[311](https://docs.rs#311)/// shared references.
[312](https://docs.rs#312)///
[313](https://docs.rs#313)/// Downstream libraries can always manually opt in to these types afterwards.
[314](https://docs.rs#314)/// (It's also less of a breaking change on our part if we re-add these).
[315](https://docs.rs#315)///
[316](https://docs.rs#316)/// TODO: Replace this with `extern type` to also mark it as `!Sized`.
[317](https://docs.rs#317)type OpaqueData = UnsafeCell<PhantomData<(*const UnsafeCell<()>, PhantomPinned)>>;

[320](https://docs.rs#320)mod tests {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    use super::*;
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    use std::ffi::CStr;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    #[test]
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    fn smoke() {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        // Verify that this library links and works fine by itself
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        let name = CStr::from_bytes_with_nul(b"abc:def:\0").unwrap();
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        let sel = unsafe { sel_registerName(name.as_ptr()) };
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        let rtn = unsafe { CStr::from_ptr(sel_getName(sel)) };
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        assert_eq!(name, rtn);
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }

# objc_protocol in objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/objc_sys/struct.objc_protocol.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct objc_protocol { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Opaque type for Objective-C protocols.

Note that, although protocols are objects, sending messages to them is deprecated and may not work in the future.

The naming of this follows GNUStep; this struct does not exist in Apple’s
runtime, there `Protocol` is a type alias of `objc_object`.

# NSInteger in objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/objc_sys/type.NSInteger.html

`pub type NSInteger = `[isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.isize.html);## Expand description

A signed integer value type.

This is guaranteed to always be a type-alias to [ isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.isize.html). That means it
is valid to use

`#[repr(isize)]` on enums and structs with size
`NSInteger`.See also the [corresponding documentation entry](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/objectivec/nsinteger?language=objc).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use core::mem::size_of;
use objc2::ffi::NSInteger;
#[repr(isize)]
pub enum NSComparisonResult {
    NSOrderedAscending = -1,
    NSOrderedSame = 0,
    NSOrderedDescending = 1,
}
assert_eq!(size_of::<NSComparisonResult>(), size_of::<NSInteger>());
```

---

# NSIntegerMin in objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/objc_sys/constant.NSIntegerMin.html

`pub const NSIntegerMin: `[NSInteger](https://docs.rs/type.NSInteger.html) = NSInteger::MIN; // -9_223_372_036_854_775_808isize

---

# NSUInteger in objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/objc_sys/type.NSUInteger.html

`pub type NSUInteger = `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html);## Expand description

Describes an unsigned integer.

This is guaranteed to always be a type-alias to [ usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html). That means it
is valid to use

`#[repr(usize)]` on enums and structs with size
`NSUInteger`.See also the [corresponding documentation entry](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/objectivec/nsuinteger?language=objc).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use objc2::ffi::NSUInteger;
extern "C" {
    fn some_external_function() -> NSUInteger;
}
```
```
use core::mem::size_of;
use objc2::ffi::NSUInteger;
#[repr(usize)]
enum CLRegionState {
    Unknown = 0,
    Inside = 1,
    Outside = 2,
}
assert_eq!(size_of::<CLRegionState>(), size_of::<NSUInteger>());
```

---

# free in objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/objc_sys/fn.free.html

## Expand description

The Objective-C runtime has several methods, usually with “`copy`” in
their name, whose return value is allocated with C’s `malloc` and
deallocated with C’s `free` method.

As such, `free` is actually also part of the Objective-C runtime.

We expose this instead of using [ libc::free](https://docs.rs/libc/latest/libc/fn.free.html), to avoid having

`libc`
as a dependency.

---

# IMP in objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/objc_sys/type.IMP.html

## Expand description

A nullable pointer to the start of a method implementation.

Not all APIs are guaranteed to take NULL values; read the docs!

## Aliased Type[§](https://docs.rs#aliased-type)

```
pub enum IMP {
    None,
    Some(unsafe extern "C"
```
[fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.fn.html)()),
}

---

# SEL in objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/objc_sys/type.SEL.html

`pub type SEL = `[*const ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[objc_selector](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_selector.html);## Expand description

An immutable pointer to a selector.

Type alias provided for convenience. See `objc2::runtime::Sel` for a
higher level binding.

---

# id in objc_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/objc-sys/0.3.5/objc_sys/type.id.html

`pub type id = `[*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[objc_object](https://docs.rs/struct.objc_object.html);## Expand description

A mutable pointer to an object / instance.

Type alias provided for convenience. You’ll likely want to use one of:

- `objc2_foundation::NS[...]`for when you know the class of the object you’re dealing with.
- `objc2::rc::Retained`for a proper way of doing memory management.
- `objc2::runtime::AnyObject`for a bit safer representation of this.

---
